text: 升旗山是檳島最高峰之一，主峰西方山海拔833公尺，也是東南亞歷史悠久的英國殖民山站，2021年更列入UNESCO人與生物圈保護區。距離喬治市不遠，完整遊覽約2～3小時。這次特別早起，5:50從飯店出發，約6:10抵達纜車站，因為人潮不多，順利搭上6:30第一班纜車上山看日出。百年纜車全長2007公尺，最大坡度達42度，約五分鐘就能抵達山頂，沿途穿梭熱帶雨林，還能看到殖民時代留下的百年洋樓，本身就是很值得體驗的旅程。抵達山頂時天色仍從黑夜逐漸轉亮，看著城市與山林慢慢被晨光照亮，景色非常迷人。山頂氣溫也比市區低約5～8℃，清晨特別舒服。若想避開人潮又欣賞日出，非常推薦搭第一班纜車上山。

This is honestly the only negative experience we have had in Malaysia. Everything else about our trip has been absolutely fantastic, but Penang Hill was a complete disappointment.

Destroys the purpose of walking in nature.

Penang Hill is one of Malaysia’s most beautiful and historically significant attractions. The scenery is breathtaking, the cool climate is refreshing, and the lush rainforest creates what should be a peaceful escape from the city.

Unfortunately, my experience was overshadowed by one major issue that the Penang State Government and Penang Hill Corporation urgently need to address.

The 2 km walk towards Heritage Cafe has become dominated by golf buggies. Instead of a relaxing nature walk, pedestrians are constantly forced to move aside for buggies travelling at unsafe speeds. Families with young children, elderly visitors and tourists are all sharing the same narrow roads with motorised vehicles that appear to have little speed control or enforcement.

It creates a dangerous environment where people cannot simply enjoy the surroundings without constantly watching for vehicles approaching from behind.

This is a serious safety failure.

One distracted child, one elderly person with slower mobility, or one buggy driver making a mistake could easily result in a severe accident. The current system appears to prioritise transporting more passengers and generating revenue rather than protecting the thousands of visitors walking through the area.

There should be strict speed limits, designated pedestrian-only sections, clearly separated buggy routes and proper enforcement. Instead, the atmosphere feels chaotic and stressful rather than peaceful.

This is not how a protected natural attraction should be managed.

The irony is that visitors come to Penang Hill to experience nature, fresh air and tranquillity. Instead, the constant movement of speeding buggies destroys that experience entirely.

The second disappointment was the Penang Hill Funicular Railway.

As the only transport system to the summit, it should be one of the highlights of the visit. Instead, it felt poorly maintained and badly managed. I paid extra for the Express Premium Pass expecting a comfortable experience, but ended up squeezed into an overcrowded train with very little personal space. The air conditioning was either not working properly or was completely inadequate for the number of passengers, making the journey hot, stuffy and uncomfortable.

The overcrowding also prevented many passengers from enjoying the panoramic views, which is one of the main reasons people take the train in the first place. The interior of the train also appeared unclean and lacking proper maintenance.

For an attraction of this international standard, charging premium prices while delivering such an overcrowded and uncomfortable experience is unacceptable.

Penang Hill deserves to be one of the world’s great nature destinations. The scenery certainly is. However, poor safety management, unregulated buggy operations and overcrowded train services significantly diminish what should be an unforgettable experience.

I sincerely hope the Penang State Government and Penang Hill Corporation take these concerns seriously. Do not wait until a serious injury or tragedy occurs before taking action. Visitors deserve a safe, peaceful and well-managed environment that reflects the natural beauty and heritage of Penang Hill.

Fantastic Family Day Out at Penang Hill! 🌿🚂
We had an amazing family trip to Penang Hill! It’s a wonderful escape into nature with cool breezes, rich history, and plenty of fun activities for both adults and kids.
🚂 The Funicular Train Ride
We took the funicular train up and down the hill (RM40 per adult). The ride itself was smooth, fast, and offered beautiful scenic views of the lush greenery as we climbed up to the top.
🛺 Insightful Jeep Tour
Once at the top, we hired a jeep ride for the whole family for RM40, and it was worth every ringgit! Our driver was super friendly and doubled as an informative tour guide. He shared fascinating historical insights about how the British colonized Penang and pointed out the various grand heritage bungalows, sharing interesting stories about which famous billionaires owned them. It made exploring the area so much more meaningful than just walking around blindly!
📸 Highlights & Kid-Friendly Fun
Animal Encounters: The kids were absolutely thrilled to meet and interact up close with a friendly capybara—definitely a highlight photo op!
Charming Vintage Spot: We loved exploring the scenic pathways and stumbling across vintage touches, like the classic red British pillar post box nestled among the lush greenery.
Overall Verdict
Whether you are here for the cool mountain air, the rich history, or family-friendly activities, Penang Hill is a must-visit in Penang. Highly recommended for families looking for a delightful mix of nature, history, and fun!

I have visited Penang Hill four times before, and today’s visit was by far the most disappointing.

A Malay female staff member suddenly shouted at us in Malay, asking why we couldn’t wait, and then called us “bodoh” (stupid). We simply turned around and looked at her, but she continued speaking to us in a rude and disrespectful manner.

No customer should ever be insulted or verbally abused. We did not cut the queue or behave disrespectfully—we simply chose not to use the optional photo service.

Penang Hill is one of those attractions that deserves a place on any Penang itinerary.

The funicular railway makes the journey to the top quick and easy, and the views across George Town, the coastline and Penang Island are spectacular. There is much more to explore at the summit than we expected, with viewing platforms, walking trails, heritage buildings, gardens, cafés and plenty of places to simply stop and enjoy the cooler mountain air.

We particularly enjoyed taking our time to walk around and explore rather than treating it as a quick trip for the view. The cooler temperature was also a welcome break from Penang’s heat and humidity.

It can become busy, particularly around the funicular railway, so arriving earlier in the day may help avoid some of the crowds. Allow at least a few hours if you want to properly experience the area rather than simply travel up, take photos and return.

A memorable Penang experience with incredible views and something for visitors of all ages. Well worth the trip.

I visited Penang Hill in the evening and it was one of the highlights of my trip to Penang. The journey up the hill by train was smooth, enjoyable, and added to the overall experience. The atmosphere at the top was peaceful and relaxing. The cool breeze made it comfortable to walk around and enjoy the surroundings, especially after sunset. One of the best parts of the visit was the spectacular night view overlooking Penang Island. Seeing the city lights spread across the landscape was truly beautiful and made the trip worthwhile. There are several viewing areas, cafés, and attractions that allow visitors to spend a pleasant few hours exploring the hill.

The natural environment is also impressive, with plenty of greenery and fresh air. It is easy to understand why Penang Hill remains one of the most popular tourist attractions in Malaysia for both locals and international visitors.

However, there is one area that needs improvement. I was disappointed by the condition of the public toilets. Unfortunately, it was not just one restroom that was affected; I found several toilets that were not clean and did not meet the standard I would expect from such a famous tourist destination. Better maintenance and more frequent cleaning would greatly improve the visitor experience.

Despite this issue, I still enjoyed my visit very much. The cool weather, beautiful scenery, and stunning panoramic views of Penang make Penang Hill a place that I would recommend to anyone visiting the island. With improved restroom maintenance, the experience would be even better and more enjoyable for all visitors.

During our short trip to Penang last week, we made time to visit Penang Hill—and it turned out to be one of the most relaxing highlights of the trip.

To get to the top, you’ll take the iconic Penang Hill Funicular Railway. Ticket prices differ for locals and foreigners—mine was around RM16, while Kelia’s was RM40. It might seem like a gap, but considering the experience, it’s still worth it.

The ride up is smooth, comfortable, and incredibly scenic. As the train climbs, you’re treated to lush greenery and sweeping views of Penang. It can get a little warm if it’s crowded, but overall, it’s a pleasant journey.

Once you reach the top, the atmosphere instantly changes—cooler air, peaceful surroundings, and stunning panoramic views. It’s the perfect spot for photos, vlogging, or simply slowing down and soaking in the scenery.

One of the highlights of our visit was dining at David Brown’s Restaurant and Tea Terrace, which truly stood out as the most memorable part of our time up there (I’ve shared a separate review just for that!).

There’s actually quite a lot to explore around Penang Hill—from nature trails to viewpoints—but since this trip was more about relaxing than hiking, we kept things simple. Think light snacks, refreshing mocktails, and desserts while enjoying the cool weather.

Pro tip: Try to head up early and come down earlier if you want to avoid the crowds. The return train tends to get much busier in the evening. That said, if you stay, you’ll be rewarded with a completely different experience—the breathtaking night view overlooking the entire Penang Island.

So many more attractions on top of the hill. A must visit place!

The Good
The main attraction is the funicular train ride—it’s a steep, swift climb with exciting views over the island. At the top, you escape the city heat with cooler temperatures and fresh air. Key spots include The Habitat (for the Curtis Crest walkway and canopy bridge), the historic Sri Aruloli Thirumurugan Temple, and a mix of colonial-era bungalows. It also offers fantastic panoramic views of George Town and the mainland.

Things to Consider
The experience can be affected by crowds, often resulting in long queues for the train, especially on weekends and public holidays. Prices for the train ticket are also considered pricey for foreigners. While there are cafes and a food court, dining options are mostly average and a bit overpriced.

Verdict
Worth visiting for the views and the cool climate. To avoid disappointment, arrive early on weekdays and book tickets online in advance.

A visit to Langkawi SkyCab and SkyBridge was one of the absolute highlights of our time in Langkawi and an experience we believe every visitor should have on their itinerary.

We purchased the Combo Ticket for RM112 per person, which included access to the SkyCab and SkyBridge, and after completing the experience we can honestly say it was worth every ringgit.

Tip: You can pay an additional RM50 for the Express Lane, but based on our experience we don't think it's necessary. The standard queue moved efficiently, and the wait time was very reasonable, making it difficult to justify the extra cost.

Located within the UNESCO Langkawi Global Geopark, the SkyCab transports visitors high into the ancient rainforest of Gunung Machinchang, one of the oldest known geological formations in Southeast Asia, with rocks dating back more than 550 million years. The journey itself is every bit as impressive as the destination.

The SkyCab is no ordinary cable car. It holds the distinction of having one of the world's longest unsupported single cable spans, stretching over 950 metres without a supporting tower. As the gondola leaves the lower station, it climbs steeply over dense rainforest, soaring high above dramatic cliffs and deep valleys before reaching the upper stations. The scale of the engineering is remarkable, and it's impossible not to appreciate the ingenuity required to build such an attraction in this rugged landscape.

The views become more spectacular with every metre of the ascent. Looking down across the rainforest canopy and out over the Andaman Sea towards the surrounding islands is simply breathtaking. On a clear day, you can even see parts of southern Thailand in the distance.

Reaching the SkyBridge is the reward at the end of the journey. Suspended high above the rainforest, this remarkable curved pedestrian bridge appears to float between the mountains. Supported by a single inclined pylon, it offers an exhilarating walk with uninterrupted panoramic views in every direction. Standing above the ancient rainforest with nothing but glass, steel and open space beneath you is an experience that's difficult to put into words.

Everything throughout the attraction was well organised, from ticketing and queue management to the friendly staff and overall presentation. Despite its popularity, the experience never felt chaotic and was managed very efficiently.

Whether you're interested in engineering, geology, photography or simply want to experience one of Malaysia's most iconic attractions, Langkawi SkyCab and SkyBridge delivers on every level. It combines world-class engineering with one of the most spectacular natural landscapes in Southeast Asia to create an experience that is both exhilarating and unforgettable.

Without hesitation, this was one of the best experiences of our travels through Malaysia, and we would recommend it to anyone visiting Langkawi.

Disclosure: We visited independently and have no affiliation with this attraction. Our review reflects our personal experience.

After 13 years away, I finally returned to Langkawi — and honestly, the island has aged like fine wine.

Now, let’s talk about the real star of the trip: the cable car.

Calling it a “ride” feels unfair. It felt more like voluntarily signing up for a slow-motion launch into the clouds. The climb was ridiculously steep, the cabin swayed just enough to keep your survival instincts fully activated, and somewhere halfway up I started questioning every decision that led me there.

To make things more exciting, there are no fans inside the cabin. Add a few nervous passengers and tropical weather, and you’ve got yourself a very authentic “sweating at altitude” experience. Parents with small children might want to prepare a pep talk beforehand — for the kids and possibly for themselves.

But then…

The doors opened, the views appeared, and suddenly none of that mattered.

Towering mountains, endless greenery, and the Andaman Sea stretching all the way to the horizon. The kind of view that makes you forget your fear of heights and immediately start filling your phone storage with photos that somehow still don’t do it justice.

Standing up there, it’s easy to appreciate the amount of engineering, maintenance, and effort required to keep this experience running. It’s impressive from every angle.

Complaints? None.

Would I do it again? Absolutely.

Would I scream slightly less on the next ride? No promises.

Langkawi, you’ve officially earned a permanent spot on my “I’ll definitely come back for this” list. Some views you admire once. Others keep calling you back.

There’s Thai food, Vietnamese food, plenty of generic junk food, things like “dragon’s breath” cereal using liquid nitrogen, and lots of souvenir and bead shops. I completely understand why this happens. Local food may not always be as commercially profitable when catering to a more international palate, but it’s still a little sad to travel all the way to Melaka and find that the main night market feels like it could be almost any other tourist night market.

That said, I did find a little gem: Ondeh Ondeh Cenderella. They sell fresh Peranakan treats and are still open during the weekend night market hours. Definitely worth seeking them out if you’re around Jonker Street.

The couple running it are getting older, so honestly, enjoy it while they’re still around and strong enough to keep doing what they do.

Otherwise, I’d say don’t feel like you have to spend your whole evening at Jonker Street. There are plenty of other good places around Melaka where you can experience much more of the local food and culture. But it's smart, keeping the tourists in one area during peak hours.

If you are visiting Melaka on a weekend, taking a night walk through Jonker Street Night Market / Pasar Malam Jonker Street is an absolute must-do experience packed with food, heritage, and culture.

​Vibrant Atmosphere & Weekend Crowd
​Every Friday through Sunday evening, this historic strip turns into a bustling pasar malam overflowing with a lively atmosphere, vibrant street stalls, and colorful busking performances. It attracts a huge crowd of locals and tourists alike. Spending 3 to 4 hours walking the full stretch and surrounding side lanes lets you soak in the electric energy, though wearing comfortable shoes is essential to handle the long stroll and tropical heat!

​Street Food Highlights: Cendol, Chicken Rice Balls & Halal Food
​The variety of local eats here is incredible:
​Local Favorites: You can cool off with authentic gula Melaka cendol or shaved ice, sample charcoal-grilled satay, or try famous chicken rice balls.
​Diverse Dining: There is an extensive selection of halal food options, Peranakan street snacks, and refreshing coconut drinks available across the market.

​Shopping & Heritage Architecture
​Beyond the food, the area is rich in historic Baba & Nyonya architecture, vibrant wall murals, and centuries-old shophouses. You will find hundreds of vendors selling unique souvenirs, local batik clothing, antique trinkets, and intricate handmade crafts.

​Whether you explore during a daytime stroll or experience the evening market buzz, it is an iconic Melaka highlight!

Jonker Street Night Market is one of Melaka’s most vibrant experiences and a must-visit if you are in the city over the weekend.

Tip: The night markets is only open on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday night. We found the best night to be Saturday as the markets extend much further out than just Jonker street.

As the sun went down, Jonker Street transformed into a busy pedestrian market filled with food stalls, local products, souvenirs, music and entertainment. The atmosphere was colourful, energetic and sometimes chaotic, but that was all part of the experience.

There was an enormous variety of street food available, from local Malaysian dishes and freshly cooked snacks to desserts, drinks and plenty of unusual options for more adventurous visitors. We enjoyed walking the length of the market, taking in the aromas and trying different foods along the way.

The entertainment added another layer to the evening. We encountered costumed characters including Iron Man, Bumblebee and Optimus Prime, while brightly decorated trishaws moved through the surrounding streets with flashing lights and loud music. There was always something happening and something new to see.

The market becomes extremely busy, particularly later in the evening, so expect crowds and take your time. We recommend arriving hungry, carrying small amounts of cash and sampling several smaller dishes rather than choosing only one meal.

Jonker Street Night Market is tourist-focused, but it remains a fun and memorable way to experience Melaka after dark. The combination of food, colour, music and entertainment created one of the most enjoyable evenings of our stay.

Jonker Street is an absolute must-visit when you're in Malacca. It's literally just a stone's throw from the Dutch Square, the Clock Tower, and A Famosa, making it easy to include all of these attractions in one leisurely walk.

While the famous weekend night market gets a lot of attention, I actually visited on a weekday and thoroughly enjoyed exploring the regular shops, most of which opened around 9:30–10:00 a.m. The streets were much more relaxed, giving me time to appreciate the beautiful Peranakan and colonial shophouses, each with its own unique façade and charm.

A definite highlight is Christina Ee, whose pineapple tarts are outstanding. Don't leave without trying their Nyonya durian cendol, the gula Melaka is rich, fragrant, and perfectly balanced. I also enjoyed the cendol at Peranakan Place, but Christina Ee's version was my personal favourite.

Take your time wandering through the heritage shops as well. You'll find beautifully handcrafted beaded shoes, traditional kebayas, antiques, and many other treasures that reflect Malacca's rich Peranakan heritage.

For food, I highly recommend Kochik Kitchen. The ayam buah keluak was exceptional, and the udang masak nanas was equally memorable. As someone with Peranakan roots, the flavours instantly reminded me of my mother's and grandmother's cooking. It was nostalgic, authentic, and one of the best Peranakan meals I've had in a long time.

If you're like me and enjoy browsing every little shop, you'll easily need a full day... or even two days, to really appreciate everything Jonker Street has to offer.

The only thing I found slightly overrated was the famous chicken rice balls. They're good and certainly unique to Malacca, but coming from Kuala Lumpur, I've honestly had better chicken rice elsewhere. It's still worth trying if you're curious, but if you only have room for one memorable meal, I'd recommend focusing on the Peranakan cuisine instead. After all, this is the heartland of Peranakan culture, and it's where you'll find some truly authentic and unforgettable food.

Overall, Jonker Street is full of history, culture, architecture, shopping, and fantastic food. I would happily visit again.

A highly recommended destination for anyone visiting Cameron Highlands. We will definitely be back again!

Genting Skyworlds Theme Park is a theme park that has a lot of potential but currently does not deliver enough to justify what visitors are paying, especially international ones. The park looks impressive on the surface with well themed areas and some genuinely good attractions that show what this place could be at its best.

The biggest frustration is that a significant number of rides and attractions were either closed or under maintenance during our visit. When you pay full price for a theme park ticket you expect to have access to the full experience. Walking around and constantly seeing barriers, closed signs, and out of service notices is incredibly disappointing. It feels like you are paying for a complete theme park but only getting access to half of one. There is no discount or acknowledgment that a substantial portion of what you are paying for is simply not available.

The pricing structure adds another layer of frustration. International visitors pay significantly more than local residents for the exact same experience. Dual pricing is something you encounter in various places across Southeast Asia and opinions on it differ, but when you are already paying a premium as a foreigner and then discover that half the rides are not even operational, the value proposition completely falls apart. You are essentially paying more than locals for less than the full experience, and that combination feels genuinely unfair.

If the park were fully operational with all rides running and the experience matched the price tag, the higher entry fee for foreigners might be easier to accept. But charging a premium while delivering an incomplete product is a tough sell that leaves a bitter taste.

Three stars because the park has clear potential and the attractions that are open are decent. But until they get all rides consistently operational and address the gap between what visitors pay and what they actually receive, this park is not delivering the value it should. Fix the availability, and reconsider the pricing disparity, and Genting Skyworlds could be a genuinely great theme park.

We went on public holiday 31 May 2026 with kids age 8 and 11.

Highlight:
Try to cover your favourite rides in the morning. If you enter at 10am, go straight to Planet of the Apes, then Epic Voyage to Moonhaven, and then Ice Age: Expedition Thin Ice because the queue is short like 5 minutes. For Independence Day and other popular rides, the queue already become 40 minutes at 10am, so use Virtual Queue instead of normal queue.

Genting SkyWorlds Review:
The entrance opened at 10am. I suggest buying the ticket online one day earlier because the price is half price, and you can also avoid the long queue at the ticket counter.

In my opinion, try your best to enter the park exactly at 10am. Once you enter, go straight to the popular rides like Planet of the Apes, Epic Voyage to Moonhaven, and Ice Age: Expedition Thin Ice. These rides are better to do early because the queue is usually shorter in the morning, and the weather is usually clearer.

We entered smoothly at 10am and straight away rushed to Planet of the Apes because there was no queue. At first, we wanted to go to Independence Day, but the queue was already around 40 minutes, so I used the Virtual Queue instead.

For Independence Day, I really suggest using Virtual Queue and booking it early. When I booked the Independence Day VQ at around 10.20am, the earliest available slot was already only at 2.40pm. So don’t wait too long to book your VQ because the good time slots can finish fast.

After Planet of the Apes, we went to Ice Age: Expedition Thin Ice, and there was also no queue. Then we went to Epic Voyage to Moonhaven. The queue was not too long, but suddenly the staff announced that the ride was temporarily closed or technical issue because it was foggy and light rain. So we went to Buck Cafe, they have lot of food variety here and delicious also.

Lesson learned: when Genting gets foggy or light rain, some rides like Epic Voyage to Moonhaven and Ice Age may close until around 3pm. So it is better to finish these rides early from 10am to 12pm, because after 12pm Genting usually becomes foggy and has light rain until about 3pm.

Since Epic Voyage was closed, we went to Bigweld’s Zeppelin and used our Virtual Queue. However, the queue was still quite long, around 20 minutes. I noticed the queue became long because they did not fully use the ride capacity. For example, there were around 5 pods with 4 seats each, which means about 20 seats total, but from what I saw, they only allowed around 10 seats, maybe about 50% capacity. This caused the queue to move slower.

After that ride, we reached Independence Day about 10 minutes early for our VQ slot at 2.40pm. But even with VQ, the queue was still long, and we waited around 40 minutes. I also noticed that the Independence Day ride seemed to use only around 50% capacity too.

The last ride is Boot Camp Training. My kids love it so much. For this ride, I set VQ at 4pm and I noticed they only allowed VQ to queue and normal queue is not allowed.

In my opinion, the waiting time could be improved if the rides used more capacity, maybe around 80%, especially during busy hours. This should help reduce the queue and make the experience better for visitors.

Overall, come early, buy tickets online before going, and use the Virtual Queue wisely. My suggested plan is: enter at 10am, go straight to Planet of the Apes, Epic Voyage, and Ice Age, then use VQ for Independence Day and other popular rides. This will make your trip easier and less stressful, especially if you come with family or kids.

The Petronas Twin Towers and KLCC are among the most impressive attractions in Kuala Lumpur and definitely worth visiting. The iconic twin towers dominate the city skyline and look spectacular from both close up and from the surrounding areas. The architecture is stunning, especially when the towers are illuminated in the evening.

The area around KLCC is clean, modern and well maintained, with plenty of open spaces where visitors can relax, take photographs and enjoy the atmosphere. The KLCC Park is a great place for a leisurely walk, with greenery, fountains and beautiful views of the towers. It is particularly enjoyable in the evening when the area becomes lively and the city lights create a wonderful atmosphere.

Suria KLCC shopping mall is directly connected to the towers and offers a wide selection of international brands, restaurants, cafés and entertainment options. There are also many food and drink choices, making it easy to spend several hours in the area.

For visitors interested in the towers themselves, the observation areas and Skybridge provide an opportunity to see Kuala Lumpur from above. The views are impressive, although tickets can be limited during busy periods, so booking in advance is recommended.

The location is also convenient because KLCC is well connected by public transportation and is easy to reach from other parts of Kuala Lumpur. There are plenty of hotels, restaurants and attractions nearby.

Overall, KLCC and the Petronas Twin Towers offer an excellent combination of architecture, shopping, food, entertainment and outdoor space. Whether visiting during the day or at night, the experience is memorable. It is a must-visit attraction for first-time visitors to Kuala Lumpur and a fantastic place for photography, sightseeing and enjoying the city skyline.

Petronas Twin Towers (Menara Berkembar PETRONAS) are Malaysia’s most iconic landmark, located in Kuala Lumpur City Centre (KLCC).

The towers were officially opened in 1999 and stand at 451.9 metres tall, with 88 floors each. They were designed by Argentine-American architect César Pelli.

For a period, they were the tallest buildings in the world — from 1998 until 2004. Today, they remain the world’s tallest twin towers.

🌉 The famous Skybridge

One of the most interesting parts is the Skybridge, which connects the two towers at Levels 41 and 42, around 170 metres above ground.

Visitors can go up to the Skybridge and continue to the Observation Deck on Level 86 for a spectacular view of Kuala Lumpur.

I’d recommend going late afternoon so you can see KL in daylight, watch the sunset, and then see the towers illuminated at night.

And don’t miss the area around KLCC Park — it’s one of the nicest places to photograph the towers.

This is the biggest climb we’ve done and echoing other reviewers it was very tiring but definitely a memorable, rewarding experience!

We started the hike at Timpohon Gate just before 9am and made it to Panalaban base camp at 330pm. We then began the last leg of the hike at approx 215am and made it to see the sunrise at the summit ☀️ We were super lucky as the sky cleared up for us to see the the incredible view! Before sunrise, we could also see the moon and many stars!!

Coming back was a real struggle for us, as it really put pressure on the legs not to mention it began pouring in our last 3km 🫣 We did finally made it back to the gate just before 4pm - we got a packaged lunch and a van was prepared to take us and other hikers back!

Prior to the hike, we made reservations on their website so the logistics to organise the hike was generally easy and smooth with consistent and efficient communication from staff - both via online leading up to the hike and a day before with reminders for mini van arrangement to and from the hotel. Also, on the van back to the hotel, we dropped a phone, and the driver very kindly pointed it out to us.

We followed their recommended packing list and had everything we needed on the hike. We weren’t too sure about drinking water so we brought extra water (and snacks too!)

Our mountain guide was quite chill but nevertheless, friendly and helpful when we needed him. He helped us navigate the more difficult paths like the rope climbing near the top and he also lent us one of his hiking poles as he noticed one of ours was too short and didn’t help much with stabilising 🫣

We were realy looking forward to doing this hike until we realised the price and how much of a tourist trap this place is.

This is Malaysia’s highest peak and the minimum price is around $800usd for services I don’t want or need.

For this price you could hike in much more beautiful places in the world.

To anyone deciding to do this hike or not, a mountain is a mountain, you don’t need to pay all that money to be out in nature, just go somewhere else.

海外登山は初参加。1泊2日で登りました。
道は整備されていて、非常に登りやすかったです。
最初は亜熱帯のジャングルから始まり、標高が高くなると雲霧林に入り、ネペンテスが多く見れる場所になります。
ジャングルを抜けると木々の背が低くなり、最終的には岩肌をひたすら登ることになります。
最後の岩肌は、しっかりした登山靴で登らないと、慣れてない人は数メートル滑落する危険性があるので注意しましょう。
私が参加した日は雨が強く、岩肌の至る所が川のようになっていたので、下手したら大怪我では済まない可能性もあります。

また、体力に自信がある人でも、ゆっくり登るのをお勧めします。

京那巴魯山(Kinabalu)海拔4095公尺，屬於東亞三神山之一，是東亞第一高峰，同時也是馬來西亞的聖山，其最大幣值100元中的圖案就是京那巴魯山。

相較於玉山為闊葉林生態，以及富士山為火山環境，京那巴魯山屬於雨林生態，登山路上可以看到如大王花及豬籠草，體驗起來非常特別。從登山口到山屋為6K，7K以前都是待在雨林裡面，一直到8K離登頂最後一哩路時會開始變陡峭，到8.5K即為京那巴魯山最高峰-羅氏峰(Low's Peak)。

如果有朋友想挑戰京那巴魯山要記住「山永遠都在，好好評估自身體力況狀再前往」，否則攀登國外的大山並不容易適應當地氣溫、濕度、地形狀況及生態環境，如果決定要前往挑戰，請務做好十足的準備，並且對山靈抱持敬畏之心，山靈才會帶給你安全給予回報。

My honest review of my climb at Mt Kinabalu. Unlike mountains like Everest, the climb is intense and packed. With a rest hut every 1-3 Km or so, but a lot of ground to cover in a single day. Your experience is also very weather dependent. Scorching weather will cause you to tire out much easier while thundery storms will bring down your morale and make your climb much more miserable.
However, with the right training, balance, thigh and calf recommended, I think the climb will be very manageable. What I enjoyed most about the climb was the rewarding buffet at the end of day one. However, the climb on day 2 is very dangerous. Climbing 80 deg walls with ropes and nothing else, I nearly died twice by loosening my grip on the rope. When I summited, I was cold and exhausted, and cold icy winds made me feel that the view wasn't worth it.
Probably what was most memorable about the climb was the memories made during the climb with my friends and family.
However, what I am thankful for was the mountain guide who guided us on what stones to step on when the ground was slippery and held my hand when I felt like giving up.
Thank you Kinabalu Park for the memorable experience on Mt Kinabalu

I booked the trek with with Seek Sophie and the staff were brilliant, swift and accommodating with responding to my enquiries, arranging my transfers and briefing us before for the trek. We were lucky to have a mountain guide for just the two of us. While we were given ample information prior and how to prepare for the trek, I was still surprised at the level of difficulty in climbing the last 3 km towards the summit. I had done ample triathlon and ocean swimming training and taken all the altitude medications before and during the climb. You have to climb in the pitch dark, with wet and windy conditions at high altitude, which also required hauling yourself up 200+ metres of roped sections and abseiling back down these ropes without harnesses. It's Sabah Parks, that mandate the rushed schedule of climbing to the guesthouse (3200m above sea level) in one day and make trekkers climb at 2:30 am the next morning to 4079m above sea level by sunrise. Our guide was very patient with us while we slowly climbed to adapt from 1800m to 4000m above sea level within 48 hours but my body needed more time to acclimatise. I am grateful our guide helped us up and down the mountain safely with both of us experiencing altitude sickness at various heights and for the beautiful views just below the summit upon sunrise. If Sabah Parks allows this, I'd recommend to allow trekkers to stay for one more night at the guesthouse to rest properly and acclimatise better before resuming the last 3 km to the summit. I'd also recommend to grade this trek as moderate to hard for experienced climbers who do not experience altitude sickness at 4000+ metres, and not as an easy or beginners trek level. Overall, I am humbled by the grandeur and power of Mt Kinabalu and now know my bodies limits at altitude. Thank you Seek Sophie for organising multiple tours for us in Borneo! They're a fantastic tour operator!

I self organised my own climb and it was significantly cheaper than using some of the extortionate tour packages. It's a bit harder to organise as there is not a ton of clear info and fully up to date websites on how to do it, but it's possible to figure it out if your fine with the added hassle. I booked 8 months in advance and got the 2nd to last spot for my trip date.

At the time of posting I paid maybe 900myr to self organise, including all relevant permits, transport to and from Mt. Kinabalu from KK, 1 night accomodation prior to the climb and guide fees etc. other tours for the same offering are going for like 2400+ to 2600+. You need to book early though to secure your panalaban hostel accommodation!!

The claim up is about 4km of mainly stairs. The trail is pretty well maintained but it's still a tough climb up, going from hot and humid jungle gradually up to more rocky terrain for the final 2km to the camp.

Camp is cold and super windy so bring lots of layers to keep you warm. It can get tough sleeping at night without warm sleepwear.

The final ascent starts at 2.30am to get you to the summit. If your fast, you get to see a beautiful sunrise after scrambling up mainly flat rockfaces with assistance ropes. The wind and cold make this a tough one, and so does the altitude.

The views are great but the peak can be busy.

Descending does wonders in your knees. I didn't take poles and highly recommend using them if you go to save some aches and pains later.

Overall it was a good challenge and a rewarding climb. The only thing I dislike is that the prices, especially for international visitors are so high. They have risen much higher than inflation due to the monopoly that a few tour companies seem to hold over the limited daily climb permits. You can check historic reviews from a few years ago to see the price gouging going on.

My recent climb to the peak of Mount Kinabalu was an exhilarating and unforgettable adventure that left me in awe of nature's splendor and my own capabilities. As I embarked on the journey to conquer Southeast Asia's highest peak, I was filled with a mix of excitement and anticipation.

The climb began at Timpohon Gate, where I was greeted by the lush rainforest enveloping the trail. Each step brought me closer to the summit, with the trail winding its way through a diverse landscape of towering trees, moss-covered rocks, and cascading waterfalls.

As the altitude increased, so did the challenge. The steep ascent tested my physical endurance and mental resilience, pushing me beyond my comfort zone. Yet, with each passing milestone, I found renewed determination to press on, fueled by the breathtaking scenery and the camaraderie of fellow climbers.

Reaching Laban Rata resthouse marked a significant milestone in the journey, offering a well-deserved respite and a chance to refuel before the final push to the summit. As night fell, I set out under a blanket of stars, guided by the light of my headlamp and the anticipation of what lay ahead.

The final ascent to Low's Peak was both grueling and awe-inspiring. Battling fatigue and altitude sickness, I pushed myself to the limit, drawing strength from the stunning sunrise painting the sky in hues of orange and pink. With each step, I felt a sense of accomplishment and wonder, knowing that I was standing on the roof of Borneo.

Reaching the summit of Mount Kinabalu was a moment of triumph unlike any other, a testament to perseverance, courage, and the power of the human spirit. As I stood at the highest point in Southeast Asia, surrounded by panoramic views of the Sabah landscape, I was overcome with a sense of humility and gratitude for the opportunity to witness such natural beauty.

Descending from the peak, I carried with me not only memories of the journey but also a newfound appreciation for the magnificence of Mount Kinabalu and the indomitable spirit of those who dare to conquer it. It was an experience that challenged me, changed me, and will forever hold a special place in my heart.

If you join via ferrata, you need to arrive the dorm in the first day by 4pm to listen to the briefing.  We arrived at about 3:35pm.  I made my money worth by listening to the breifing and tried using the climbing protections. :)

After the briefing, we went to have a buffet dinner.  You need to sleep by 7pm because you need to wake up at 1:30am to climb up thr hill.  Many people cannot sleep well, but really better to take a rest, even for 3 hours only.  While climbing up, you can see the sky with milky way 🌌 (but not tto obvious).

To get the certificate, you need to arrive the check point before 5:30am.  I arrived at about 4:35am and was at KM 8.0 5:40am.  A while later, the sky starts to get brighter with some beautiful colours while you can still see a lot of stars.  The scene was stunning and it was a really peaceful moment to me.

Resting for a while, I keep moving.  With the help of the tour guide (thank you so much!), I reach the peak at 6:59am.  The road to the peak was really strep and need to be careful.  I need more time if I climbed it up myself.

Then we go back to the dorm.  After some rest, we went down to our starting point.  It took us about 5 hours for the 6km route.  And we arrived at about 5:10pm.  If you arrive at the entrance after 4pm, extra charge is needed to pay to the tour guides (30 RM per hour for each tour guide).  We paid 120 RM for the two tour guides.

Anyway, reaching this mountain is one of my accomplishment in my life :). (May not have the second chance to do it again)

Really enjoyed visiting Kellie’s Castle! I’ve always loved classical buildings with centuries of history behind them, and this place definitely has that kind of charm. Kellie’s Castle – ghé “lâu đài ma” giữa vùng ngoại ô Ipoh

Cách trung tâm Ipoh khoảng 30 phút lái xe, Kellie’s Castle nằm ở Batu Gajah, bang Perak, là một trong những điểm tham quan có màu sắc khác biệt nhất của Malaysia. Công trình được khởi xây đầu thế kỷ XX bởi William Kellie Smith, một chủ đồn điền người Scotland. Ông qua đời năm 1926 khi lâu đài vẫn chưa hoàn thành, để lại phía sau một công trình dang dở và hàng loạt câu chuyện bí ẩn.

Tôi đến đây vì cái tên “lâu đài ma”, nhưng điều giữ chân lâu hơn lại là cảm giác vừa đẹp vừa buồn của một giấc mơ bị bỏ lại. Những bức tường gạch cũ, hành lang dài, cầu thang dẫn lên tầng cao, các căn phòng chưa hoàn thiện tạo nên một không gian có phần lạnh lẽo. Người ta kể về những bóng người xuất hiện ở hành lang hay căn phòng cũ, nhưng đứng giữa ban ngày, nỗi sợ không rõ rệt bằng cảm giác tò mò về cuộc đời chủ nhân và lý do công trình mãi mãi dừng lại ở trạng thái dang dở.

Điểm thú vị là du khách có thể tự mình len qua nhiều khu vực của lâu đài, lên tầng cao ngắm vùng cây xanh xung quanh Batu Gajah và tìm những góc kiến trúc pha trộn ảnh hưởng châu Âu, Ấn Độ và Moorish. Một vòng tham quan hợp lý mất khoảng 1–2 giờ.

Hiện Kellie’s Castle vẫn hoạt động bình thường. Trang chính thức công bố mở cửa hằng ngày từ 9h30 đến 22h, lượt vào cuối lúc 21h30. Giá tham khảo gần đây cho khách nước ngoài khoảng 10 ringgit/người lớn, 8 ringgit/trẻ em, nhưng nên kiểm tra lại khi mua vé vì chính sách có thể thay đổi.

Kellie’s Castle was one of the more unusual historical places I visited in Perak. It does not feel like a typical restored palace or museum because the building was never actually completed. Standing inside the unfinished structure, with its empty rooms, long corridors, arches and partially developed sections, gives the place a slightly mysterious atmosphere that is quite different from most heritage attractions in Malaysia.

The mansion was built by William Kellie Smith, a Scottish planter who became wealthy through rubber and tin-related businesses in Perak. Construction began in the early 20th century, with major work taking place around 1915. Unfortunately, Smith died of pneumonia in Lisbon in 1926, and construction was subsequently abandoned. His unfinished residence eventually became one of Batu Gajah’s best-known landmarks.

The architecture is probably the strongest part of the visit. There are Moorish, Indo-Saracenic and Roman influences throughout the building, with horseshoe-shaped arches, brickwork, decorative details and unusual structural features. The mansion was also planned to have an elevator, which would have been an impressive feature for its time. Some of the hidden rooms and underground passages add to the sense of mystery surrounding the property.

I enjoyed exploring the different levels because the unfinished condition actually makes the building more interesting. Instead of everything being perfectly restored, you can see parts of the original construction and imagine what the completed mansion might have looked like. The elevated location also provides pleasant views of the surrounding greenery and the Raya River area.

The main drawback is that some areas can feel a little rough and the historical information could be presented more clearly. The stories about ghosts and supernatural activity are popular, but I think the verified history of William Kellie Smith and the people who built the mansion is much more interesting than relying only on the haunted-castle reputation.

Overall, I found Kellie’s Castle genuinely worthwhile. It is not an enormous attraction and the visit does not need an entire day, but the unfinished architecture, unusual history and atmosphere make it memorable. I would recommend visiting with some background knowledge because understanding why the castle was built and why it remained unfinished makes walking through it much more meaningful.

An Emerald Sanctuary: The Golden Era of Kellie’s Estate
Long before Kellie’s Castle became an intriguing set of ruins perched above the modern highway, it was chosen for a very specific reason: its breathtaking, panoramic location.
​When William Kellie Smith surveyed the land in the early 1900s, he didn't just see a site for a mansion; he saw a private kingdom wrapped in an endless blanket of green. Positioned high on a gentle hilltop, the estate was designed to command sweeping 360-degree views of Perak’s lush landscape—a tropical paradise that felt worlds away from the rest of the world.
​A Living, Breathing Canvas
​In its prime, standing on the upper terraces or looking out through the mansion's ornate window frames offered a view that rivaled the finest estates in Europe:
​The Sea of Greenery: Looking outward, your gaze would travel across rolling emerald lawns that sloped gracefully down toward the riverbanks. Beyond the estate grounds stretched vast, thick rubber plantations and pristine tropical jungle, creating a vibrant sea of green under the wide, blue Malaysian sky.
​The Gentle River: Winding quietly at the base of the hill, the Sungai Raya added a soft, sparkling ribbon to the landscape. From the upper floors, watching the sunlight bounce off the water as it curved around the property gave the entire estate a tranquil, resort-like feel.
​The Misty Horizon: Far in the distance, the dramatic limestone hills of the Kinta Valley rose sharply against the horizon. On clear mornings, a soft layer of fog would linger around their bases, giving the impression that the castle was floating above a sea of clouds.
​A View Designed for Royalty
​The architecture was intentionally crafted to bring this magnificent scenery indoors:
​Natural Picture Frames: Every keyhole arch, circular portal, and wide balcony was positioned like a living frame. Sitting in the planned rooftop entertainment area, guests would have been treated to a constant cool breeze sweeping up the hill, carrying with it the fresh scent of rainforest leaves and damp earth.
​A Timeless Sanctuary: It was a place designed for quiet morning coffees and golden hour strolls along the elevated walkways, where the contrast between the warm, red brickwork and the brilliant green surroundings created an unforgettable backdrop.
​Today, while nature has slowly softened the edges of the old brick and yellow stone, that magical green view remains largely unchanged. Standing on the rooftop terrace, feeling the wind rustle through the surrounding treetops, you can still easily imagine how breathtaking this hill must have felt a century ago—a true Scottish dream nestled in the heart of the tropics.

Beyond its striking design, the castle is surrounded by intriguing legends and historical stories, making every corner worth exploring. Learning about William Kellie Smith's vision and the castle's rich past adds a special dimension to the visit.

What makes Kellie's Castle even more memorable is that it stands as a symbol of love and devotion, built with the dream of creating a grand home for his beloved wife and family. The combination of architectural beauty, historical significance, and romantic legacy makes this place both inspiring and unforgettable.

Kellie's Castle (Istana Kellie) has an interesting history and unique architecture, but unfortunately the overall experience was quite disappointing. The building itself is impressive and has great potential, but the place feels poorly maintained and does not fully live up to its reputation.

The biggest issue is the condition of the castle and surrounding area. Some parts look neglected, with signs of aging, limited restoration, and areas that could be cleaner and better managed. The atmosphere is interesting, but at times it feels more like an abandoned building than a properly preserved historical attraction.

The information about the history is interesting, but the visitor experience could be improved with better explanations, more interactive displays, and better facilities. The heat, insects, and lack of comfort also make the visit less enjoyable, especially during the daytime.

For the entrance price and the effort needed to travel there, I expected more. The castle has a fascinating story and beautiful architecture, but the lack of proper maintenance prevents it from reaching its full potential.

Overall, Kellie's Castle is an interesting place for history lovers and photography, but I would not consider it a must-visit attraction. It feels overrated, and with better preservation and management it could become a much more impressive destination.
